head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: If total fuel is less than total cost, no start works
A global feasibility check that lets the loop find the answer without a second pass
Net fuel change at station i
Reduce two arrays to one array of gains
Fuel left since the candidate start
Cannot get from `start` to `i + 1`: abandon this start
Next station becomes the candidate; empty tank

blocks.h: Why can we skip all stations between the old start and the failure?
p: If we start at `s` and first run out of fuel at `i`, any station `k` between `s` and `i` fails earlier or at the same point: reaching `k` from `s` left us with a non-negative tank, so starting at `k` with an empty tank has at most that much fuel and fails at or before `i`. So the next candidate jumps to `i + 1`.

blocks.h: Why is the answer valid at the end?
p: After the global check, total fuel ≥ total cost, so some start exists. The candidate from the last reset has a non-negative balance until the end of the array. The part before it has total net ≤ 0 (that is what the resets said), so the global sum ≥ 0 means the suffix sum covers it on the wrap-around: the circuit completes.

bullets: Time: O(n), one pass for sums and one for the scan.
Space: O(1).

134.takeaway: Gas station greedy: if the total is non-negative a solution exists; reset the start to i+1 whenever the running tank goes negative.

head: Code

rows: Bits that have appeared once (mod 3) so far
Counting each bit position modulo 3 using two bitmasks
Bits that have appeared twice (mod 3) so far
A 2-bit counter per bit position: states 00, 01, 10
Toggles bits: adds 1 in `ones` when the bit was 0
Clears bits that are in `twos` (they just moved to the next state)
Bitwise AND with the complement of a mask
Bits that appeared 1 time mod 3 are exactly the unique number's bits
Everything else appeared 3 times and cancelled

p: `[2, 2, 3, 2]` (binary `10`, `10`, `11`, `10`). Each bit position is a tiny state machine: 0 → 1 (ones) → 2 (twos) → 0.

A bit seen 0, 1 or 2 times (mod 3) has three states, which need two bits to store. `ones` and `twos` together form that 2-bit counter for all bit positions at once; XOR alone (problem 136) works only when the repeat count is 2, because then one bit of state is enough.

blocks.h: Why the order of the two lines matters
p: `twos` is updated using the already-updated `ones`. That ordering encodes the transition table correctly: a bit entering `twos` must be removed from `ones` first. Swapping the lines breaks the state machine.

bullets: Time: O(n).
Space: O(1).

137.takeaway: Count each bit mod 3 with two bitmasks (a two-bit counter per bit position); XOR cancels pairs, this cancels triples.

Finding the middle of a linked list without knowing its length

p: `1→2→3→4→5`. Three phases: find the middle, reverse the second half, weave.

The target order takes nodes alternately from the front and the back. A singly linked list can't walk backwards, so we reverse the second half to be able to traverse it from the tail. That gives O(1) extra space; the alternative of pushing nodes into a list or stack costs O(n).

After the split the first half is at least as long as the second (it gets the middle node for odd lengths), so the second half runs out first. For `1→2→3` the second half is just `3` and the loop runs once; the first half's last node already ends the list because its `next` was cut.

bullets: Time: O(n), three linear passes.
Space: O(1) extra, relinking nodes in place.

143.takeaway: Reorder list = find the middle (slow/fast), reverse the second half, then merge the two halves alternately.

Meaning

rows: A dict that counts; missing keys start at 0, so `slopes[k] += 1` just works
Tallying how many times a key appears
Greatest common divisor (from `math`): reduces a slope fraction to lowest terms
Using an exact fraction as a dict key instead of a float
Reduced dy; exact because `g` divides it
Canonical sign so `1/-2` and `-1/2` are the same key; vertical lines get dy positive
Most points sharing a slope from point i, plus point i itself
Only later points, since earlier pairs were already counted from their own anchors
Avoiding double counting (copies the list, O(n))

p: `[[1,1],[2,2],[3,3],[1,4]]`. For each anchor, slopes to the later points are counted as reduced `dy/dx` pairs.

blocks.h: Why reduce with gcd instead of using dy/dx as a float?
p: Floating division can make two equal slopes differ in the last bit, or two different slopes look equal (for large coordinates). A reduced integer pair is exact and hashable. Also dividing by `dx = 0` would crash for vertical lines; the pair `(1, 0)` represents them safely.

blocks.h: Why is counting from one anchor enough?
p: All points on a line through the anchor share that slope to the anchor. So within one anchor, equal slopes mean collinear with it. The line's best count is found when the anchor is its leftmost point in input order, because the later points are the ones scanned.

bullets: Time: O(n²) pairs, each with a `gcd` (O(log C) for coordinate size C).
Space: O(n) for the counter of one anchor.

149.takeaway: Max points on a line: for each anchor, count points per exact reduced slope with gcd and a Counter; the best count + 1 is the answer.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Persistent buffer of characters that were read from the file but not yet handed to the caller; it lives on the object, so it survives between `read` calls
State that must outlive a single call
Provided API (Application Programming Interface): fills up to 4 characters into `tmp` and returns how many it actually read
The only way to reach the file
Don't append the unused slots of `tmp`
A short read means end of file; stop asking for more
How many characters can really be returned
O(1) removal from the front, in order
FIFO (First In, First Out) buffer; a list `pop(0)` would be O(n)

p: File `"abcdefg"`, three calls `read(3)`, `read(5)`, `read(2)`. 'Reads' is the number of `read4` calls inside that `read`.

blocks.h: Why a buffer that persists between calls?
p: `read4` always consumes 4 characters from the file. After `read(3)` the 4th character `d` has already left the file, so if it isn't saved the next call loses it. The queue holds those over-read characters for the next caller. In the single-call version (problem 157) no buffer is needed because nothing carries over.

blocks.h: Why `while len(self.q) < n` instead of a fixed number of reads?
p: The loop reads only until the buffer holds at least `n` characters. A call that the buffer can already satisfy (for example `read(1)` while `d` is left over) makes no `read4` call at all, and we never read more than one chunk past what is needed.

bullets: Time: O(n) per call.
Space: O(1) beyond the buffer, which never holds more than 3 leftover characters between calls.

158.takeaway: Read-N-characters with repeated calls: keep an instance-level queue for over-read characters so nothing from `read4` is lost between calls.

Meaning

rows: Bucket width = the smallest the max gap can be (pigeonhole): n numbers spread over a range have a gap of at least (hi-lo)/(n-1)
Choosing a bucket size so the answer can never be inside a bucket
Number of buckets needed to cover `lo..hi`
Ceiling-style division by +1 on the integer range
Smallest and largest value that landed in each bucket (`None` = empty)
Only the extremes of a bucket matter
Mapping a value to its bucket
Gap from the previous non-empty bucket's max to this bucket's min

p: `[3, 6, 9, 1]`: lo=1, hi=9, n=4, so size = max(1, 8 // 3) = 2 and count = 5. Buckets:
Walk left to right, comparing each bucket's min to the previous non-empty bucket's max.

blocks.h: Why can the answer ignore gaps inside a bucket?
p: Pigeonhole: n values over (hi - lo) have some adjacent pair at least (hi - lo)/(n - 1) apart, which is at least the bucket size. Any pair inside a bucket is closer than that (at most size - 1 apart), so the maximum gap must cross a bucket boundary, and only the min and max of each bucket matter.

bullets: Time: O(n), linear passes only; no sort.
Space: O(n) for the buckets.

164.takeaway: Maximum gap in linear time: bucket by the minimum possible gap; by pigeonhole the answer lies between bucket neighbours, so keep only each bucket's min and max.

head: Code
Meaning

rows: Stack of ancestors whose left spine we have entered but not yet visited
Pushes `n` and all its left descendants, so the smallest unvisited value ends on top
The next smaller element is always down the left spine
The top is the next in-order value
After visiting a node, queue up its right subtree's left spine
Everything in the right subtree comes next, in order

p: BST (Binary Search Tree) `7 / (3, 15 / (9, 20))`. Stack shown bottom → top.

blocks.h: Why a stack and not a list of all values?
p: Flattening the tree into a list on construction is O(n) time and O(n) space up front. The stack stores only the current left spine, at most the tree height h, and does the work lazily.

blocks.h: Why is `next()` O(1) amortised and not O(1) worst case?
p: A single call may push many nodes (a long left spine). But every node is pushed once and popped once over the whole traversal, so n calls cost O(n) in total, which is O(1) per call on average.

bullets: Time: O(1) amortised per `next`/`hasNext`.
Space: O(h), where h is the tree height.

173.takeaway: Iterative in-order traversal as an iterator: keep a stack of the left spine; after popping a node, push the left spine of its right child.

p: `[3, 30, 34, 5, 9]` → strings. Some of the pairwise decisions the sort makes:

blocks.h: Why compare `a+b` with `b+a` instead of comparing the numbers?
p: Plain numeric or lexicographic order fails: `30` vs `3`. Numerically 30 > 3, but `3` then `30` gives `330` while `30` then `3` gives `303`. The right question for the final number is which concatenation order is larger, which is exactly `a+b` vs `b+a`.

It is a total preorder (transitive): `a+b ≥ b+a` defines a consistent ranking, so sorting with it is well defined and the greedy order is optimal. Checking transitivity is what separates a correct custom comparator from a buggy one.

bullets: Time: O(n log n) comparisons, each costing O(L) for string length L.
Space: O(n · L) for the strings.

179.takeaway: Largest number = sort strings with the comparator `a+b > b+a` via `cmp_to_key`; handle the all-zeros case.

blocks.h: Why loop over `t` inside each price?
p: Each day we can advance each transaction count by at most one step: buy for transaction t uses the profit of t-1 transactions, sell uses today's buy. Doing the updates for increasing `t` on the same day also allows buy and sell on the same day, which is harmless (profit 0).

Binary arithmetic: subtracting 1 borrows from the lowest 1

Counting or removing set bits, one per loop

p: `n = 11` (`1011`): each step removes the lowest 1.

blocks.h: Why is this better than testing every bit?
p: The shift-and-test loop (`n & 1`, `n >>= 1`) runs once per bit position (up to 32). Brian Kernighan's trick runs once per set bit, so `1000…0` takes one step.
`n = 0` returns 0 because the loop body never runs. Python's built-in `n.bit_count()` (3.10+) or `bin(n).count('1')` give the same answer in one line; mention them, then show the loop.

bullets: Time: O(k), where k is the number of 1 bits (at most 32).
Space: O(1).

191.takeaway: Brian Kernighan's trick: `n &= n - 1` clears the lowest set bit, so the loop runs once per 1 bit.
